cands.name: Scott Singer
cands.bio: Republican nominee in FL-25. Lawyer; Boca Raton city council member then mayor 2018-2026 (term-limited). Born in Miami Beach, raised in Fort Lauderdale; Pine Crest School, Harvard, Georgetown Law (campaign site). Chairs the America First Policy Institute Mayors' Council.
cands.local_ties: Says he has lived in the district for 40 years and on the barrier islands for 20+ years; Boca Raton resident (campaign site).

record.text: Boca Raton mayor 2018-2026 and earlier council member; says he voted seven straight times to lower the property tax rate and launched 21 red-tape streamlining initiatives (his own claims; not independently verified).
Voters rejected the One Boca downtown redevelopment plan in the March 10, 2026 referendum by roughly 74%; Singer had backed advancing the contract to voters.

Campaign platform at the Oct 20, 2026 forum: bar institutions that take foreign money from federal funds, supports Trump's Iran war and benefit of the doubt on temporary Russia-sanctions suspension; claims Moskowitz violated the STOCK Act.

money_notes.text: Wikipedia's FL-25 page says the race drew over $42.2 million in spending as of Oct 2026 (citing Punchbowl News, Oct 6, 2026). I could not break it down by donor or super PAC.

controversies.text: Jewish Insider reported Singer traveled to Qatar in 2024 with a U.S. mayors' delegation tied to the World Economic Forum and was photographed with Qatar's minister of municipality; who paid was not clear. His campaign says he came away with a better understanding of U.S.-Qatar relations and that he would introduce a bill barring federal funds to schools receiving foreign money; spokesperson said he 'does not share all the views of all who attended.'

foreign_ties.text: 2024 trip to Qatar as part of a U.S. mayors' delegation (see controversies); payer unclear in reporting.

endorsements.text: Donald Trump (announced Sept 1, 2026 on Truth Social, calling him an 'America First Patriot').

Per Wikipedia's FL-25 section: Gov. Ron DeSantis, former Rep. Peter Deutsch (a Democrat), Ben Shapiro, NRCC, National Association of Police Organizations, NFIB, U.S. Chamber of Commerce, Republican Jewish Coalition; earlier backers include Rep. Steve Scalise and Florida AG James Uthmeier.

cands.gaps: Only 2 council votes verified (others, e.g. Brightline station lease and millage votes, lacked a retrievable roll call naming his vote). Super PAC spending in FL-25 not itemized. Moskowitz-related claims on his page are his own.

votes.bill: Introduction of the 99-year Terra/Frisbie 'City Center' downtown lease contract (Jan 2026)
votes.what: Advanced a 480-page agreement to lease about 7.8 acres of city land near the Brightline station for apartments, condos, a hotel and offices; it would only take effect if voters approved it in a March 10, 2026 referendum (voters rejected it, about 74% no per WPTV).
votes.result: passed 3-1 (Andy Thomson no; one member absent)

votes.bill: Charter amendment lengthening council terms from three to four years (Dec 2022)
votes.what: Placed on the ballot a proposal Singer himself made to extend council and mayoral terms; voters rejected it on March 14, 2023 (about 59% no).

cands.name: Jared Moskowitz
cands.bio: Democrat; U.S. Rep. since 2023 (FL-23), running in new FL-25 after the remap. Lawyer; Parkland commissioner 2006-2012; Florida House 2012-2019; state Emergency Management director 2019-2021; Broward County commissioner Jan-Nov 2022 (appointed by DeSantis). Won 2026 primary with 63.5%.
cands.local_ties: Born in Coral Springs (1980); lives in Coral Springs with his wife and two children (Wikipedia).

record.text: Committees (119th Congress): Foreign Affairs (ranking member, Oversight and Intelligence subcommittee) and Judiciary; co-chairs the Bipartisan School Safety and Security Caucus.

Reintroduced the EAGLES Act (Secret Service threat-assessment work on school violence) with Rep. Mario Diaz-Balart; sponsored the Robert Levinson memorial in the FL House; only Democrat to join the DOGE caucus.
In Nov 2024 a suspect with a rifle and a manifesto was arrested near his home in what Moskowitz described as a potential assassination plot (Reuters, cited by Wikipedia).

money_notes.text: Wikipedia's FL-25 page says the race drew over $42.2 million in spending as of Oct 2026 (citing Punchbowl News). AIPAC and other pro-Israel groups have endorsed him (WLRN forum report); Singer's side points to his stock portfolio, which he says an outside group manages.

controversies.text: Stock trades: a trust account for his children sold $65,000-$150,000 of Seacoast Banking shares on March 10, 2023, the day Silicon Valley Bank failed, after he attended a congressional briefing that day (NYT/Sun Sentinel via Wikipedia); in 2025 disclosed purchases across twenty companies, which his spokesperson said an outside advisor made. Singer alleges STOCK Act violations; Moskowitz says he follows all rules. No finding of a violation appears in the sources I opened.

endorsements.text: Per Wikipedia's FL-25 section: National Education Association, Giffords, League of Conservation Voters Action Fund; AIPAC, DMFI and Jewish Democratic Council of America among primary-stage groups.

cands.gaps: Votes limited to 5 of the FL House roll calls I could open and read (2013-2014 and 2018 votes beyond SB 7026 not pulled). Super PAC breakdown for FL-25 not obtained. Congressional votes are filled elsewhere. Campaign site/social accounts not verified.

votes.what: Requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft, burglary or assault of a police officer, and lets states sue over immigration enforcement.

votes.bill: H.R. 1968 (2025) Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025
votes.what: Funds the federal government through September 30, 2025 at roughly prior-year levels (March 2025 stopgap).
Requires documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.

votes.bill: H.R. 1 (2025) One Big Beautiful Bill Act (final passage)
votes.what: The 2025 reconciliation law: extends the 2017 tax cuts, adds new tax breaks, cuts Medicaid and food-assistance spending, and raises defense and border spending and the debt limit.

votes.bill: H.R. 881 (2025) DHS Restrictions on Confucius Institutes and Chinese Entities of Concern Act
votes.what: Bars Homeland Security funds going to Confucius Institutes and entities tied to the Chinese government.

votes.bill: H.R. 152 (2025) Federal Disaster Assistance Coordination Act
votes.what: Streamlines coordination among federal agencies delivering disaster aid (hurricane/flood recovery).

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Sept. 19 House passage)
votes.what: House-passed stopgap funding bill to keep government open through Nov. 21, 2025; stalled in the Senate and a shutdown began Oct. 1.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Nov. 12 final, ended the shutdown)
votes.what: Ended the 43-day federal shutdown: funds government through Jan. 30, 2026 and three full-year spending bills.

votes.bill: S. 1071 / FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act (final)
votes.what: Final FY2026 defense policy and funding-authorization bill (about $900 billion), carried in the House on the vehicle S. 1071.
Final FY2026 spending package funding most remaining federal agencies through September 30, 2026.

votes.bill: CS/SB 7026 (2018) Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School Public Safety Act
votes.what: Gun, school-security and school-safety package passed after the Parkland shooting; Moskowitz helped draft it.
Changed conditions for voluntary and informed consent before an abortion (reported as adding a 24-hour waiting period).
Protects churches and certain individuals from being required to perform or serve same-sex marriages when it conflicts with religious convictions.

Broad K-12 bill: charter-school capital funding, principal scholarship program, virtual instruction and rules for low-performing schools; $418.95 million appropriation. He also voted Nay on the House's first passage on 2017-04-13 (79-38).
Proposed constitutional amendment capping consecutive service of Florida Supreme Court justices and appeals judges at 12 years; died in the Senate.
